Recent strikes have also reached the Baltic and waters off Libya, while a maritime risk zone was extended on Nov. 18 toward Romania and Bulgaria. The disruption is raising freight and insurance costs and shifting grain purchases toward European suppliers, but prices are moving unevenly: Euronext’s December wheat contract closed Nov. 23 at €240.25 a tonne, up €3.50, while Constanța bread-wheat and corn quotes fell 1.7% and 1.3%. More Argentine and Australian wheat could become available to buyers in coming weeks.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] Powerful El Niño nears December peak as droughts, fires threaten crops
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization says the powerful El Niño underway in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and likely persist through February 2027, disrupting rainfall and raising drought and flood risks worldwide. Sea-surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region rose from 1.6°C above normal in June to 2.5°C above normal in August; forecasters project temperatures about 3.7°C above normal in October-December, exceeding the previous record of 2.6°C above normal. Recent impacts include drought and fires in Brazil, extensive forest fires in Indonesia, and a possible 21% to 25% decline in Ivory Coast cocoa output. Researchers attributed Indonesia’s July-October rainfall deficit largely to El Niño, while saying human-caused climate change made the atmospheric conditions about three times more likely and more intense. The United Nations Development Programme says acting now to limit the impacts would cost $36 billion, compared with $73 billion if action is delayed.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] IEA says Iran shock speeds electrification but may prolong coal use
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The International Energy Agency says the energy disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is accelerating countries’ shift toward electrification. The agency said 25 countries had announced new electrification-related policies since February as governments seek more domestic energy sources. At the U.N. climate talks, COP31, host Türkiye is pressing to raise electricity’s share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035; draft negotiating text does not specify that the added power must come from renewables. The IEA also said buildings now use more energy for cooling than for heating, a shift it links to rising temperatures and demand for air conditioning. The agency expects solar and nuclear power to gain ground, but energy-security concerns could keep coal in use as backup, particularly in coal-rich Asian economies. It warned that inadequate electricity grids, charging infrastructure and supply capacity could slow electrification.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items.title: [franceinfo.fr] Macron weighs January vote on French constitutional budget rule
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

President Emmanuel Macron is weighing whether to revive a 2011 constitutional budget amendment and convene France’s lawmakers in Congress in January to reassure investors over borrowing costs and a deficit the government has struggled to reduce. Macron told Le Figaro he would explore the proposal if market volatility persisted into January; he is also watching whether lawmakers pass the 2027 budget by year-end. France expects a 2026 deficit of 5.4% of gross domestic product, while public debt is about 119% of GDP. The proposal would require multi-year plans to restore balance rather than impose an immediate numerical deficit ceiling. Both houses approved the 2011 text, but it never went to a final vote in Congress. Adoption at Versailles would require three-fifths support from lawmakers. Even if the constitutional change passes, lawmakers would need to adopt an organic law defining how the framework works, followed by a first budget framework law. Macron’s January decision remains conditional on market volatility and the budget debate; lawmakers would still need to establish the measure’s implementing rules.

Both houses approved the 2011 text, but it never went to a final vote in Congress (franceinfo.fr, 20minutes.fr). Adoption at Versailles would require three-fifths support from lawmakers (ft.com). Even if the constitutional change passes, lawmakers would need to adopt an organic law defining how the framework works, followed by a first budget framework law (radiofrance.fr). Macron’s January decision remains conditional on market volatility and the budget debate; lawmakers would still need to establish the measure’s implementing rules (franceinfo.fr, radiofrance.fr). Bond movement: French government bonds outperformed euro-area peers on Monday, pushing the 10-year yield down 0.09 percentage points to 4.79%; it reached 5% last month, its highest level since 2002 (ft.com). German comparison: Germany’s constitutional debt brake, in force since 2016, limits the federal structural deficit to 0.35% of GDP except in extraordinary circumstances; Berlin loosened the rule last year to allow higher defense spending (lesechos.fr, pb.pl). EU benchmark: The EU’s Stability and Growth Pact sets a 3% of GDP deficit threshold, and France is under an excessive-deficit procedure while its forecast remains above that level (nouvelobs.com).
